jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:35:31 t V
In addition to Newton's Laws, this week we'll look at common forces - gravity, friction, and tension. We'll see some of the most common types of problems that pop up on the F=ma exam.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:35:54 t V
Our big idea is to use extremes and special cases.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:36:03 t V
When we want more intuition for a problem, it helps to ask things like "What if mass AA is really, really huge?" or "What if we turn off gravity?" Those cases tend to be simpler, and after thinking about them, the original problem often makes more sense.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:36:11 t V
For example, suppose we have a half-Atwood machine with top mass MM and hanging mass m,m, but to make it more complicated, the pulley has moment of inertia II and radius R.R.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:36:13 t V




jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:36:46 t V
How many of you could solve this using free body diagrams and Newton's 2nd law?
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:37:19 t V
It might be hard to guess the magnitude of acceleration a,a, but we can look at an extreme case by imagining the bottom mass becoming very small.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:37:32 t V




jonjoseph 2025-06-25 19:37:36 t V

very large (a≫g)(a≫g)
gg
very small (a≪g)(a≪g)
something else

The mass mm is too small to pull much, and there will be very little acceleration, a≪g,a≪g, and in the limit, as m→0,m→0, we have a→0.a→0.

a?=g(m+M)IR2+m+Ma=?g(m+M)IR2+m+M

yes

am→0?=gMIR2+Mam→0=?gMIR2+M

The strings are massless, so the net force each has to be zero. We exert force FF downward on the bottom string, and the mass has to exert a force FF upward on the top. By Newton's Third Law, the force from the mass on the bottom string is the same as the force from the bottom string on the mass, which is what we call TB.TB. So TB=F.TB=F.

The strings have some elasticity. The tension in them only increases when they stretch. Since the top string is connected to the mass, its tension only increases as the mass moves. It takes some time for the mass to move, so there's lag in TTTT increasing as we suddenly increase F.F.

If you stand at rest on a bench, the bench exerts a normal force on you, equal and opposite to your weight. Which force is related to this normal force by Newton's third law?

(b)

(d)
(e)

jonjoseph 2025-06-25 20:45:33 t V
Choice (a) say these two are a third-law pair:

- normal force (bench to you)

- gravity (Earth on you)
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 20:45:44 t V
If we draw a free body diagram, these forces are equal and opposite.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 20:45:46 t V




jonjoseph 2025-06-25 20:46:02 t V
If you jump onto the bench, then while you're landing, there's a big spike in the normal force from the bench to you, just like the big force the ground exerts on a bouncing golf ball. Since these forces aren't always equal in magnitude, they aren't a third-law pair.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 20:46:20 t V

jonjoseph 2025-06-25 20:46:58 t V
Newton's third law tells us |FA on B|=|FB on A|.|FA on B|=|FB on A|. One force is a force on object AA and the other force is a force on object B.B.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 20:47:07 t V
The third-law pair of a force from the bench on you is a force from you on the bench. That's (c).

Summary
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:03:49 t V
That's all for class this week. You'll practice these problems, and a couple of other small ideas (like ropes with mass) in the homework. Next week, we'll cover another common class of questions on the F=ma: those about energy and momentum.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:03:55 t V
When solving a problem, we often use variables throughout our work, even if the problem gives numbers. Then, when we get a formula for our answer at the end of the problem, we can examine extreme cases, such as setting the friction coefficient to zero or setting two masses equal to each other, to see if the formula holds up.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:04:00 t V
Newton's second law, F=ma,F=ma, means that when things suddenly change speed (such as a bouncing golf ball), there must be a large force to generate that change in speed.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:04:06 t V
Newton's third law always finds pairs of the form force of A on B = force of B on A.force of A on B = force of B on A. If two forces both act on the same object, those forces might be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, but they aren't a third-law pair.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:04:11 t V
Normal forces are forces that are "normal" (perpendicular) to some surface. They're often vertical forces between the ground and an object sitting on the ground, but they don't have to be.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:04:16 t V
On inclined planes, it usually is best to choose coordinates pointing down the inclined plane (x),x), and perpendicular to the plane (y).(y). The component of gravity pointing down the plane is mgsinθ,mgsin⁡θ, and the normal force, assuming the inclined plane is fixed and the object is sitting on the plane with no other forces pushing in the direction of the plane, is mgcosθ.mgcos⁡θ.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:04:20 t V
The magnitude of kinetic friction force is μkN.μkN. For static friction, the maximum possible force is μsN,μsN, but the force can be less than this.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:04:23 t V
Objects like ropes, string, and springs can be under tension. A rope under tension TT exerts a force TT on objects at either end of the rope. If the rope is massive or if there is friction on it, the tension in the rope can vary along its length. In most problems, the tension in the rope is uniform.
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:04:31 t V
When a rope wraps around a pulley, it exerts a force on the pulley. This is a normal force, so there can also be friction involved!
jonjoseph 2025-06-25 21:04:59 t V
Good job. Lots of stuff! Stay safe and see you next week.
